historical_overview.text: Canoe Lake Cree First Nation is a Cree community in northwestern Saskatchewan whose land-based history predates Treaty 10. Hunting, fishing and trapping sustained community members across a broad traditional territory before and after treaty signing.

On September 19, 1906, Chief John Iron and Headmen Baptiste Iron and Jerome Couilloneur signed Treaty 10 at Île-à-la-Crosse, according to the commissioner’s report, with the Crown’s commissioner, James Andrew Joseph McKenna.
The creation of the Primrose Lake Air Weapons Range in 1954 restricted access to approximately 75% of the Nation’s most productive traditional lands. A subsequent claim was settled in June 1997.
These documented events describe part of the Nation’s treaty-era and later history; treaty records are not a complete account of its older Indigenous history or continuing Cree identity.

significant_historical_events.title: Primrose Lake Air Weapons Range
significant_historical_events.description: The range’s establishment removed access to about three quarters of the Nation’s most productive traditional lands, disrupting land-based livelihoods.

significant_historical_events.title: Claim and settlement
significant_historical_events.description: Canoe Lake submitted a claim in 1975 for the loss of traditional territory. Canada accepted it in 1995, and a settlement followed in June 1997.

historical_connections.name: English River First Nation
historical_connections.description: Chief William Apisis signed Treaty 10 at Île-à-la-Crosse on August 28, 1906. The English River and Canoe Lake bands participated in the same 1906 treaty process.

historical_connections.name: Clear Lake Band
historical_connections.description: Chief Raphael Bedshi-Dekkge signed Treaty 10 in 1906 for the historical Clear Lake Band, another participant in the original negotiations. Later known as the Peter Pond Band, it divided in 1972 into Buffalo River and Turnor Lake, now Birch Narrows Dene Nation.

records.connections_note: These are shared historical treaty relationships. The historical Clear Lake Band is distinct from today’s Nations; these links do not imply common language, ancestry, governance or a political alliance.

research_notes.text: Signing location: McKenna’s contemporary report places the Canoe Lake band’s September 19 signing at Île-à-la-Crosse. A later OTC account lists Canoe Lake. The location above follows the contemporary report; the date is consistent across these accounts.
